text: A dirty read happens when your transaction reads data that another transaction has written but hasn't committed yet -- and that other transaction then rolls back. You end up having read a value that, in the end, never really existed in the database at all.
Here's the timeline. Session A starts a transaction and updates a product's price, but doesn't commit -- the change sits open, neither committed nor rolled back.

Session B, running under READ UNCOMMITTED, queries that same row while Session A's transaction is still open. It gets back 9999.00 -- Session A's in-flight, uncommitted change -- immediately, with no waiting at all, because READ UNCOMMITTED skips honoring Session A's lock entirely.

Now Session A rolls back. The price change never happened. Session B's 9999.00 has no committed history behind it whatsoever -- that's the dirty read. Not stale data, not a timing coincidence -- a value that, as far as the database is concerned, never existed.

This can only happen under READ UNCOMMITTED, because every stricter level requires reads to only see committed data. You'll also see the same risk requested per-query with a table hint: WITH (NOLOCK) has the exact same dirty-read-permitting effect as running the whole session under READ UNCOMMITTED.

Dirty reads are the first and most severe of the three classic anomalies. Next lesson, the second one: the nonrepeatable read, where a value changes between two reads in the same transaction because someone else's commit landed in between. See you there.
